## The checker's report

Check of the Boo-Boo Vet design sheet, round 1 (file ``games/boo-boo-vet/ART.md` as checked`, lines 1 to 223)

Records: all twelve named records and the one "not used" exist; code, scope, standing and check state are as the lookup prints today (all `confirmed`, no Dutch core goal, so no regime).
Limits: every limit the sheet takes is in that record's Limits; three places go beyond a record or past a neighbour without saying so (findings 3, 4, 5), and one statement about the whole pack is not true (findings 1, 2).
Levels: levels, sub-bands, basis (`official` for us-ca, `convention` for nl), the cross-grade and end-of-primary labels and "no gap" are as printed at ages 3, 4, 5 and 6; headings are all there in order; rulings 4 and 8 hold (first-visit default open at both ends; all 30 cells have a sound and no column shares one).

## Findings

**1. The records, line 172.** It says no record in either jurisdiction carries reading a need in an animal, which is a statement about the whole pack and is not true of it (see finding 2), and "four of the five pairs" rests the droop-and-bowl pair on records that carry only that water is a need. Replace the paragraph with:

> What none of the records named below carries, in either jurisdiction: that a need can be read in an animal. Every feelings record below is about people, and none names a state of the body such as a sore paw, cold, an itch or thirst. Animals come in only through the care records, which name no signs. Injury, illness and treatment are in none of them. So the animal as the one who is read, the five signs, and the pairing of each sign with its care are the game's own design; of the five cares, only water is named by a record.

**2. The records, us-ca, line 191.** "The nearest" is wrong: grade 1 has four lanes, and its science lane holds `us-ca 1-LS1-2` (state-board-adopted-standard, confirmed today), which is nearer on the animal side than 1.1.5.P. Replace the paragraph with:

> Not used: no record of the `grade-1` lanes is named. Two come near. `us-ca 1.1.5.P` (state-board-adopted-standard, confirmed) is about telling the signs of a few common illnesses in people and stops before treatment; the game shows no illness. `us-ca 1-LS1-2` (state-board-adopted-standard, confirmed) is about working out, from texts and media, patterns in what young animals and their parents do that help the young stay alive, with the signals of the young and the parents' answers as its examples; there the one who answers is the parent, and the child reads about it. The game is designed from neither.

**3. The records, us-ca, line 181 (`us-ca 1.8`).** The limit is taken correctly, but the next sentence then claims "one simple answer" under it for the first position; a give is helping, which this record's Limits put at the later age only, so for a three-year-old the give is beyond the record and must be marked as the game's own choice (pack: education, limits-come-from-the-limits-section.md). Replace the line with:

> &nbsp;&nbsp;Limits taken: at the earlier age only shared feeling and concern, with no helping mentioned; comforting and helping come at the later age, where an adult's support is now and then needed. So what this record carries for a child of the earlier age is the stroke of the hand, which is concern and never a care that is judged, and which works at every position. Giving a care is helping, which the record names at the later age only: the first position still asks for one give toward one need, and for a child of the earlier age that give is beyond this record and is the game's own choice.

**4. The records, nl, line 200 (`nl Open staan voor de emoties van een ander / 4`).** The record's Limits point to a neighbouring bullet for recognising that others have needs; the sheet rests "a need the child notices" on this record without looking the neighbour up, and does not mark that the met need is beyond it. Replace the line with:

> &nbsp;&nbsp;Limits taken: an offer, as above; "basic" bounds it to one simple reaction, and nothing says the child meets the need; which needs, and whose, is not said. So at the first position one tap is the whole answer; that the animal is then well is beyond this record and is the game's own choice. This record's Limits give recognising that others have needs to a neighbouring bullet of the same card (`nl Ontdekken van de eigen kwaliteiten en krachten / 3`, curriculum-institute-guidance, confirmed), which asks for no action; it was looked up, and it is not among the records the claim names.

**5. Where the two differ, lines 212 to 215 (ruling 6).** Four points do not say which jurisdiction the game follows or that nothing in the play depends on the difference, and line 213 calls one give "the narrower reading of each" although under `us-ca 1.8` the narrower reading is concern alone. Line 216 stands. Replace the four lines with:

> - **Which feelings.** The `us-ca` foundation 1.3 gives basic emotions as examples and sets no number. The `nl` fase 1 card names four and says the others are children. The game follows neither list, so nothing in the play depends on the difference: its five states are its own choice, three of them (hurting a little, bothered, worn out) are named by no record, and the two it shares with the Dutch four are named under `nl` above.
> - **How far the youngest child goes.** At the earlier age the `us-ca` foundation 1.8 stops at concern and names helping only later. The `nl` peuter card asks for a basic reaction to a need and does not say the need is met. These are different bounds on different statements. At its first position the game follows the `nl` bullet: one need, answered by one act. Under `us-ca` 1.8 that act is help, which is named at the later age only, so for the youngest child the give is beyond that record and is the game's own choice; what 1.8 carries at the earlier age is the concern of the stroke. That the need is then met is beyond the `nl` bullet and is the game's own choice too.
> - **Which care is named.** The `us-ca` records name water (3.7 at the earlier age, K-LS1-1 among its examples) and give sleep as an example at the later age. Of the `nl` records, the two that ask for care with animals name no care task, and the fase 1 card names water, food and a place. The game takes water, which is named under each heading, so nothing in the play depends on the difference: the bowl as the care of its first pair rests on the `us-ca` records and on the `nl` fase 1 card, each under its own heading, and the droop as its sign and the other four pairs rest on no record.
> - **Standing.** The `us-ca` records are foundations, two adopted standards, and one statement of voluntary guidance. The `nl` records are all guidance of the curriculum institute and none is law. Nothing in the play depends on the difference; the claim uses each standing's own word and puts the two sets in separate sentences.

**6. The claim, line 222 (ruling 1).** The second paragraph puts both jurisdictions' records in one list of what "these records carry", words it in the Dutch records' terms ("treating animals with care" is not what `us-ca 3.7` carries), leaves out that 1.8 carries helping at the later age only and that the telling and describing of the two adopted standards are not in the game, and again rests "four other pairs" on the pair. The first paragraph (line 220) stands. Replace line 222 with:

> What the `us-ca` records carry, and all the game is designed from in them: recognising how simple feelings show in another person (`us-ca 1.3`; `us-ca 3.B.1` for the cues of face and body, its naming of the feeling not being in the game); concern for what someone in distress needs and, at the later age only, comforting and helping (`us-ca 1.8`); kind ways of showing another that one cares (`us-ca K.7.2.M`, whose telling is not in the game); and that animals have to be looked after and that water helps them stay alive (`us-ca 3.7`; `us-ca K-LS1-1`, whose describing is not in the game). What the `nl` records carry, and all the game is designed from in them: reading the outward signs of simple feelings in someone else, one basic reaction to another's need, treating animals with care, and that animals need water. Under both headings the feelings records are about people, and none names a state of the body such as a sore paw, cold, an itch or thirst. That a need can be read in an animal from how it moves, the five signs, and the pairing of each sign with its care are the game's own design and rest on no record; of the five cares, only water is named by a record. The game makes no statement about what any child has learned or can do.

**7. The representation, line 69.** The research file is misreported: it cites three sources for this strand, not one, and what it did not find is a study of an app teaching a child to regulate feelings or carry out a self-care routine. Replace the paragraph with:

> **Trial or practice.** This is school and nursery practice without a trial behind it. The research file calls the evidence for this strand thin and mostly about programmes with adults: training children to reason about what others think and feel works in controlled studies, media about feelings helped where a parent talked with the child about it, and it found no controlled study showing that an app by itself teaches a young child to regulate feelings or to carry out a self-care routine. Its advice for the strand is marked as inference, and its rows for naming feelings and caring for others cite no trial of the representation. So the game is rehearsal: it is built on a representation in common use, and nothing is claimed for it beyond that.

**8. The grid, line 37.** "Every other cell ... one step more plainly" includes the hand's five cells, which line 48 says move no step. Replace the paragraph with:

> Six objects: the five care things and the child's own hand. Five actions: giving the object to an animal that limps, that shivers, that scratches, that droops, or that hides. One cell in each column helps, and it is marked. Every other cell of a care thing works, is funny, and shows the need again one step more plainly, in the place the wrong thing landed. The hand's five cells are strokes: they help no need and move no step.

**9. The error as a consequence, line 88, and three cells of the grid (lines 41 and 42).** The count is wrong (30 cells, 5 help, 5 are strokes: 20 care-thing cells do not help, not 24); "a wrong thing stops short of it" is contradicted by the plaster that lands on the hiding animal's nose and the blanket that covers it and makes "the whole lump" tremble; and the "whine" of the sore-pawed animal breaks line 16's "no crying in pain". Replace line 88 with:

> - **As interesting as success.** Each of the twenty cells in which a care thing does not help is its own small comedy, and the animal is bewildered or tickled by it, never hurt and never worse off. A frightened animal is never pressed: no thing pulls it out, uncovers it or follows it, a wrong thing comes to rest at the edge of its hiding place or over it and never on the animal, and its trembling never grows.

Line 41, last cell (plaster, hides):

> It lands beside the nose that peeks out; the nose sniffs it and pulls in, and two eyes blink in the dark. A tiny tick, a sniff.

Line 42, first cell (blanket, limps):

> Tucked in, but the sore paw sticks out of the blanket and waves. A soft whump, a small questioning hum going up.

Line 42, last cell (blanket, hides):

> The blanket settles over the hiding place and the lump under it goes on trembling, no more than before. A whump, a cloth rustle that does not stop.

**10. The toy, line 28 (ruling 5).** "Lies where it was dropped" stays in the world, but `things` stores only "one of a few named spots". Replace the sentence "Let go elsewhere and the thing lies where it was dropped and can be picked up again." with:

> Let go elsewhere and the thing slides to rest on the nearest of the few named spots on the table and the floor, lies there, and can be picked up again.

**11. What is stored, line 123 (ruling 5).** The well scene is filled from "the things that did not fit in the order they were tried", but `table` stores only how many; after a put-away in the middle of a patient that list cannot be rebuilt. Replace the line with:

> - `table`: the patient on the table, or none. A patient is its animal, where it was laid out (a position id), its one or two needs, each with the step its sign is at and whether it is met, how many cares did not fit (stored as 0, 1 or 2, where 2 means two or more), the care things that did not fit, each once and in the order first tried (at most five), the things its cart carries, and whether it came from the carrier.

**12. What is stored, new bullet after line 129 (ruling 5).** Several things the sheet leaves on an animal or in the room are in no field and are not said to be short-lived: the foam beard (which day 15 lists beside the den and the boat), fur on end from the crackling blanket, brushed fur, drops on the lamp, the dimmed lamp, the mouse's fallen hat, older plasters. Add:

> - Not stored, and so short-lived: whatever a reaction leaves on an animal or in the room that is in no field above (a foam beard, fur on end, fluffed or brushed flat, drops on the lamp, the lamp dimmed for a rest, the mouse's fallen hat, a hiding animal's one step out, a plaster older than the two newest). Each is shaken off, settles or is put right before that reaction ends, and none is there on load.

**13. The scenes, lines 157, 158 and 160 (ruling 5, and "How a cycle restarts").** No scene's "saved at the start" names the fields it changes, scenes 2 and 4 have none at all, and scene 4's cause does not say what a touch on the one who waits does while the patient on the table still has a need (a toddler will do this at once; the idle ladder already assumes the answer). Line 160 also sends the animal out "with what helped it" while line 87 says no care thing leaves the cart. In line 157 replace the last sentence "The outcome is saved when the scene starts." with:

> *Saved when the scene starts:* in `table` the need marked met; `finished`; `position`, moved if the judgement moves it; and `things` (the care that landed lies on the patient; a plaster on the paw is rebuilt from the need marked met).

At the end of line 158 add:

> *Saved when the scene starts:* `made` (what the pair makes) and `things` (where its two things lie); for a well animal given the thing it loves, `things` alone.

Replace line 160 with:

> 4. **Coming in** (3 to 4 seconds, and never in the way of a touch). *Cause:* with the table empty or the patient on it well, the child touches the one who waits, or the carrier. While a need on the table is unmet, a touch on either is answered where it stands (the one who waits looks up and shows its sign once more, the eyes at the window blink) and nobody comes in. *Beats:* the animal on the table hops down and goes out to the garden with what helped it, its own to keep; the one who waited walks in the way its need makes it walk and climbs onto the table; the cart rolls in behind it, carrying every thing of the new layout. *Saved when the scene starts:* `garden` (the animal that goes out and what helped it; a fourth pushes the oldest out), `table` (the one who comes in), `finished` (cleared), `waiting` and `drawn` (the next patient, laid out from the stored position, when the one at the door came in), `carrier` (none when it was touched; laid out again as "A harder option the child picks" says, with `drawn`), and `things` (each thing the new cart carries lies on the cart again). `made` is not changed: what was made of a thing comes in with it.

(The sheet does not say what coming in does to `things` and `made`; the replacement states the reading that agrees with lines 87, 109 and 129. If the design is otherwise, the list must still name both fields and say what happens to each.)

**14. The designed order, line 115.** "A carrier sometimes stands" leaves the harder option to chance and gives no rule for when it is laid out, against "the child may always choose it" in the same sentence and against the pack's question on a wanted thing that comes by luck (pack: game-design, the-line-between-depth-and-manipulation.md; "The hidden position"). Replace the line with:

> - **A harder option the child picks.** From `basket` on, and at every position but the last, a carrier stands beside the one who waits, shut, with two eyes at its window. It is laid out from the same stream, one position above the stored one, whenever a patient comes in and no carrier stands there. It looks harder because less of the animal can be seen, and the child may always choose it by touching it; the one who waits stays where it is. A carrier cycle is judged like any other.

**15. The grid, line 54, and the designed order, line 113.** The one who waits shows a need and can be given things, but the sheet does not say what happens when it is given the thing that fits; whichever way it is built, either the fitting care is seen not to help (against line 146 and "the rules stay the same", pack: game-design, depth-from-combinations.md) or a patient is made well outside a cycle. Replace line 54 with:

> - **On the mouse, and on the one who waits**: each reacts where it stands. The mouse wears a plaster as a hat. Mischief works. The one who waits takes a thing as play, by its taste, and its sign stays at its step whatever it is given: a need is met on the table only. The one thing that would fit its need is never used on it there: held out at the door, it is sniffed and nosed back toward the table, so the care that fits is never seen not to help.

In line 113 the last sentence stands as it is.

**16. The characters, lines 146 and 142.** A taste reaction may not look like a sign: "a dog with a sore paw is helped by the plaster and still does three steps of the boot walk" shows a limp-like walk straight after the limp was helped, against line 89 ("the limp is gone") and against the rule that when a character's body is the working object nothing else about it varies (pack: game-design, working-objects-stay-plain.md). Replace line 146 with:

> - **A taste never decides whether a care helps, and never looks like a sign.** The care that fits a need always helps, for every animal. The taste decides how the animal takes it: a thirsty cat drinks by dipping a paw and licking it; a dog with a sore paw is helped by the plaster, walks sound at once, and then stops to give the plaster one long suspicious sniff. No taste reaction uses the place and movement of a sign (a held-up paw, a shiver, a scratch, a droop, a hide), so an animal that is well never looks as if it had a need. A thing that does not fit plays its grid cell in that animal's manner: the one that loves it enjoys it for a moment before the need comes back, the one that is wary ducks it.

In line 142 (Dog), replace the "Is wary of" cell with:

> the plaster: sniffs it at arm's length, sneezes, and backs round it in a circle
